text:
Did the AI bubble just burst, or was this only a scare? On Thursday, November 5, 2026, the stock market had its worst day since the tariff crash of April 2025. Almost $3 trillion in value was gone in one day. Micron fell more than 17%, Nvidia more than 9%, and the market's fear gauge, the VIX, jumped almost 70%.

In China, the AI bubble has already burst: its AI stocks fell about 40% in under four months. So was Thursday the final crack of America's AI bubble, or the start of a bigger stock market crash, or neither? This update explains what happened, why it fell so hard, whether that's normal, and how to tell the difference. The AI bubble explained like you're 5.

In this video:
🗳️ The election, 41 local votes, and why a vote about data centers hits chip stocks
📉 Micron, Nvidia and Google: why they fell, and why Google barely did on Thursday

text:
Same age. Same pay. Same $100,000 saved. Max buys a house. Leo rents one just like it and invests the difference. Who's richer after 20 years?

In America, the typical homeowner is worth about $396,000. The typical renter? About $10,000. So renting must be the worst money decision you can make. Right? We followed Max and Leo for 20 years with today's prices and today's mortgage rates to find out what's really going on.

In this video:
🏠 What buying a $417,500 home really costs per month: about $3,200, almost half of a typical paycheck before taxes
🧾 The myth: in his first month, only about 8% of Max's costs build something he owns
📒 Year 3: why selling costs (about 8%) wipe out most of Max's gain
📈 Year 10 and year 20: who's ahead, with careful and historical numbers for stocks and homes
⚠️ The big catch: the renter only wins if he really invests the difference, every month
🧮 One simple number to check your own town: the price-to-rent ratio, and why the interest rate can flip the result

There's no answer that fits everyone. But after this video, you'll know the two honest questions that decide it for you.

text:
Why can't anyone copy ASML? One Dutch company is the only one on Earth that can build the EUV machine behind every new phone chip and every advanced AI chip. It costs about $400 million, ships in 250 containers and seven jumbo jets, and fires 50,000 drops of melted tin every second.

It started in 1984 in a leaky wooden shed in Eindhoven. The first machine leaked oil and flopped, and its own owners wanted out. Experts later called the light inside today's machine "stupid" and "crazy". This is the story of ASML, explained like you're 5: a young engineer who stayed for forty years, a Japanese scientist a whole room laughed at, and a light everyone said was impossible.

In this video:
🏚️ Eindhoven, 1984: the project nobody wanted
🔬 How a chip is printed with light (a city on your fingernail)
🧱 The climb: oil leaks, a Lego-like machine and two tables that beat the giants
💧 The water trick that saved Moore's Law (for a while)
😂 EUV lithography: the light experts laughed at, and the man who came back
🕯️ Ten years of failure, three candles and one flight that saved everything
☀️ Inside the machine: a tiny sun, the smoothest mirrors on Earth, a printer off by 5 atoms
🌍 Why nobody can copy ASML, and why the US and China fight over it

Not a prediction and not financial advice. Just the story of one company the whole world quietly depends on.

text:
One cent on your pillow. Every midnight, it doubles. You can stop whenever you want, but once you press stop, it's over forever. Which day would you stop?

Pick your day at the start and watch what it gets you. Day 9 buys you a loaf of bread. Day 28 makes you a millionaire. By day 56 you have more money than the whole world earns in a year. And Rita, the baker, still won't sell you a single loaf.

Penny explains it like you're 5: what doubling really does, why the real world starts sending you letters once the money gets big, and why new money that nobody worked for makes everything more expensive. That's inflation.

In this video:
🪙 Why doubling looks boring for 20 days and then explodes
🚗 Buying a car in cash: why the dealer has to report you
🏦 Why a bank only guarantees $250,000 per person
🧾 Found money is taxed: the couple who found $4,467 in an old piano
🎁 Big gifts need a tax form
🍞 More money, same bread: how inflation happens

text:
Is the US debt a Ponzi scheme? So many of you called America's $40 trillion debt exactly that. So we went back to the man the word is named after: Charles Ponzi.

In 1920, Charles Ponzi promised 50% in 45 days, and a crowd stormed his office to get their money back. He handed out coffee and doughnuts, and many of them stayed. Weeks later, it was over. He arrived in America with $2.50 and died with $75.

America also pays old IOUs with new ones. So is the national debt the same machine? We check it line by line, with a tiny village, a man named Gary and his Duck Futures. A Ponzi scheme and the US national debt, explained like you're 5.

In this video:
🎩 The Charles Ponzi story: how a few cents per coupon became millions

A coffee costs $1 at breakfast. One week later, the same coffee costs about $2,353. That really happened: in Hungary in 1946, prices doubled roughly every 15 hours.

Today inflation is much slower, but you've felt it too. A basket of everyday things that cost $100 at the start of 2020 costs about $130 today. And in September 2026, US gas prices jumped 9% in a single month. So where does inflation actually come from, who wins, who loses, and can anyone stop it?

Penny explains it like you're 5. We shrink the economy down to a tiny village with one baker: Rita bakes 100 loaves a day, the village has 100 coins, and then the mayor quietly makes 100 more.

In this video:
🍞 The 3 causes of inflation: too much money, too few things, and people expecting higher prices
💸 Germany 1923: a loaf of bread went from 250 marks to 200 billion marks
🇭🇺 Hungary 1946: a banknote with 20 zeros, and a new money worth 400 octillion old pengő
⚖️ Who wins and who loses: why savers lose and borrowers win, including governments
🛑 How the Fed stops inflation, and why Paul Volcker's 20% interest rates hurt so much
🎯 Why the target is 2%, not zero

Nobody can tell you where prices go next. But after this video, you can answer all three questions yourself.
